lesson.title: sort(): Putting a List in Order, Permanently
lesson.summary: How .sort() reorders a list in place and returns None, how reverse=True flips the direction, and why it differs from the sorted() function, which leaves the original list untouched.
lesson.body:
The last method in this unit brings back, one final time, the return-value habit you have been building since the List Methods overview: sort mutates the list it is called on and returns None, exactly like append, insert, and remove. It is also the method beginners misuse most often, typically by writing something like new_list = old_list.sort(), expecting new_list to hold the sorted result, and instead getting None, because the sorting already happened in place on old_list before that assignment ever ran.

The syntax is list.sort(). With no arguments, it arranges the list's elements from smallest to largest, using whatever natural comparison makes sense for the element type: numbers sort by value, and strings sort lexicographically, meaning character by character according to each character's underlying code point.

scores = [72, 95, 81, 60, 88]
scores.sort()
print(scores)

scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)

Trace the numbers first. scores starts as [72, 95, 81, 60, 88]. Calling sort() with no arguments rearranges it in place into ascending order: [60, 72, 81, 88, 95], which is what the first print shows. Calling sort(reverse=True) rearranges the current list into descending order instead, giving [95, 88, 81, 72, 60], shown by the second print. reverse is a keyword argument that flips the direction of the comparison; it does not simply reverse whatever order the list happened to be in beforehand, it resorts from scratch in the opposite direction.

Sorting strings holds a surprise worth seeing directly, because it exposes exactly how the default comparison works.

names = ["Blake", "amir", "Zoe", "diego"]
print(sorted(names))
print(names)

Every character has a numeric code point behind it, and in that scheme, every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase letter: "B" is 66, "Z" is 90, while "a" is 97 and "d" is 100. Comparing the names by their first character's code point, "Blake" (66) sorts before "Zoe" (90), which sorts before "amir" (97), which sorts before "diego" (100). So sorted(names) prints ['Blake', 'Zoe', 'amir', 'diego'], an order that looks strange until you remember it is comparing character codes, not alphabetical position in the everyday sense. If case-insensitive alphabetical order is what you actually want, sort accepts a key argument, such as key=str.lower, that tells it to compare a transformed version of each element rather than the raw element itself.

This example also demonstrates the second half of this concept: sorted() is a built-in function, not a method, and it returns a brand new sorted list while leaving the original completely untouched. print(names) after the call above still shows ['Blake', 'amir', 'Zoe', 'diego'], in its original, unsorted order, because sorted(names) never modified names at all; it only handed back a separate sorted list. Choosing between list.sort() and sorted(list) comes down to the same question you have been asking all unit: do you want to change the list you already have in place, or build a new one and leave the original alone.
